summary.en: Matt stresses that layoffs must be delivered one-on-one by a manager, never by email or group message, to preserve dignity and avoid backlash. He shares frameworks for running companies transparently and the famous "Mochary method" for CEO effectiveness. The episode is a master class in humane, high-accountability leadership.
summary.zh: 马特强调，裁员必须由直属上级一对一当面告知，绝不能用邮件或群消息，以保留尊严、避免反弹。他分享了透明运营公司的框架，以及著名的"莫查里方法"CEO 效能体系。本期是关于"有人情味、又高度担责"的领导力大师课。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: The biggest marker that I've seen between a botched layoff and a successful layoff is at the moment someone hears that they no longer have a job, did they hear it from their manager in a one-on-one? If that's when they heard it, it'll be okay. But if they heard it in an email, in a group chat, in any kind of thing where they were sitting next to or they're hearing it along with other people, it wasn't personalized, it wasn't one-on-one, that is terrible. That's when people get really angry and that's when they start going on to Twitter and going to newspapers and et cetera, because it feels dehumanizing. It feels like you didn't give a shit about me. You don't even have the courtesy to tell me to my face. And of course, there's no way to allow that person to express their emotions because they're in a group. So, that's the most important thing.
turns.zh: 我见过的最明显的裁员失败与成功之间的区别在于，当一个人得知自己失业时，是经理一对一告知的吗？如果是这样，那还好。但如果是通过邮件、群聊，或者在其他人面前宣布的，这就太糟糕了。这种方式缺乏个性化和一对一沟通，令人感到不被尊重。人们因此会感到愤怒，进而在推特、报纸等平台上发声，因为这让人觉得自己被无视了。更重要的是，在这种集体场合下，人们无法释放情绪。这才是最关键的区别。

turns.zh: 好的。我的职业生涯丰富多彩。最初在互联网1.0时代创办了Totality公司，取得了不错的财务成果。之后玩了很久，接着投身社会公益，帮助刑满释放人员通过成为卡车司机获得并保住工作机会。这段经历非常有趣，但我意识到自己想念同行，想重返科技领域。但不想再创业，因为创业太耗费精力，最终结果是赚大钱，而我当时并不需要钱。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: And so I thought, how could I get in the tech world and not actually have to do the hard work? Oh, I could be a coach. I could coach people and then I just get to do the fun stuff and advise them and then they have to do the hard work. And so I looked around and thought, well how could I do that because I'm not a coach and so why would anyone listen to me? Then someone told me that there were students at Stanford that had started companies but no one would coach them. They couldn't get into YC because YC doesn't accept students. So, I went and started coaching them and it was super fun and very successful and then they started recommending me up the food chain and eventually, I met folks like Naval Ravikant and Sam Altman and Brian Armstrong and they recommended me around to the rest of the tech community, and ended up coaching some of the CEOs and the leaders of the biggest tech companies and biggest tech investment firms.
turns.zh: 于是我就在想，怎样才能进入科技领域，又不必亲自去干那些苦差事呢？哦，我可以当教练啊。我可以指导别人，这样既能享受乐趣，又能给他们出谋划策，而具体工作就交给他们去完成。于是我四处打听，心想：但我又不是教练，谁会听我的建议呢？后来有人告诉我，斯坦福大学有些学生创办了公司，却找不到人指导。他们又进不了Y Combinator（YC），因为YC不招收学生。于是我开始指导他们，过程既有趣又成功。后来他们又把我推荐给其他人，最终我结识了Naval Ravikant、Sam Altman和Brian Armstrong等业界大牛，他们又把我推荐给科技界的其他领袖，最终我指导了一些科技巨头和顶级投资公司的CEO。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: It's been a ton of fun and for me, I do things for joy and each and every one of these interactions has been massively joyful for me and the people I coach become my really close friends, so it's all very selfish on my part.
turns.zh: 这真是件乐事。我做事都是为了快乐，每次与被指导者的互动都让我满心欢喜，他们也成了我的挚友，所以说这一切对我而言都是利己的。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Right on.
turns.zh: 说得好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. You have a lot of fans on Twitter and the internet and ahead of this chat I polled folks on Twitter and asked them what they would ask you if they were chatting with you, so I thought I'd start off with asking you a few those questions and then we'll dig into a few very specific topics that I'm excited to talk about. The first question comes from Leo Polovets who's a GP at Susa Ventures, and he asked, "Matt has coached some incredible founders, what are some of the most common areas where even the most successful founders still struggle?"
turns.zh: 太棒了。你在推特和网络上有很多粉丝。在这次聊天之前，我在推特上询问大家，如果能和你聊天，会问什么问题，所以我想先问你几个他们提出的问题，然后再深入探讨一些我特别感兴趣的话题。第一个问题来自Susa Ventures的普通合伙人Leo Polovets，他问：“Matt指导过一些非常出色的创始人，即使是最成功的创始人也会在哪些方面遇到困难？”

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Great question. To me, the bar is fear and how strongly do people feel fear? There are few people that I coach that just don't feel fear at all. And frankly with them, we have very tactical conversations, but they're the minority. The most feel fear to some degree, some feel it a lot, some feel it less, but when they feel it grips their mind and it prevents them from seeing... It prevents them from doing the thing that is difficult but necessary, so that's a lot of what our coaching is, me pointing out to them, hey, I think you're in fear.
turns.zh: 好问题。在我看来，关键在于恐惧感，以及人们对恐惧的感受有多强烈？我指导的有些人根本不感到恐惧。说实话，和他们交流时我们会谈论很务实的话题，但他们是少数。大多数人都会在某种程度上感受到恐惧，有些人感受强烈，有些人感受较弱。但当恐惧占据他们的思维，阻碍他们看清现实……阻止他们去做那些困难却必要的事情时，这就是我们指导工作的重点——我会提醒他们：嘿，我觉得你现在很恐惧。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: What happens is very early on in coaching they'll go, yeah, okay, I'm in fear. So what? I go, great. I believe that fear is actually giving you bad advice and I think you're predicting that if you do this A will happen. Well, I'm predicting that if you do that, the exact opposite will happen. So, I'll tell you what, why don't we make a bet? This is very high stakes, why don't we pick something that's lower stakes? You make a prediction, we'll see if I make the opposite and then let's bet on it. So we pick something and then we make a bet on it, and whoever wins the bet in the future gets to determine what the actions are.
turns.zh: 事情是这样的，在教练指导的初期，他们会说："是啊，好吧，我现在很害怕。那又怎样？"我会说："太好了。我认为恐惧实际上会给你错误的建议，而且你预感到如果做这件事A会发生，但我预测如果你做那件事B，完全相反的情况就会发生。所以，我跟你说，不如我们打个赌吧？风险太大了，不如选个风险低一点的。你预测结果，我们看看我是否能预测出相反的结果。然后我们选个事情打赌，未来谁赢了谁来决定后续的行动。"

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: I've made this bet hundreds of times and so far, I've never lost. It's not because I'm magician or a genius, it's because when someone's in fear, they're gripped. They can't see reality, their brain is making very exaggerated predictions. Whereas when someone is not in fear, and I'm not because it's not my situation, I am not gripped and therefore, my brain isn't making exaggerated predictions. And so, we make this bet once I win, then all of a sudden the CEO realizes, oh my God, there's something to this, fear gives bad advice. Then after that, all I need to do is remind the person that I perceive them to be in fear. That's all it takes, and they're like, oh, okay, and then they go ahead and do the thing that they feel fear about. Then of course, later they come back to me and say, Matt, that was magical. It works so well.
turns.zh: 我已经打过上百次这样的赌了，到目前为止从未输过。这不是因为我是个魔术师或天才，而是因为当人们处于恐惧中时，他们会被恐惧控制。他们看不清现实，大脑会做出夸大其词的预测。而当一个人不处于恐惧中时——我不是这种情况——他们就不会被恐惧控制，因此大脑也不会做出夸大其词的预测。于是，我们打赌。一旦我赢了，首席执行官会突然意识到，天啊，这说法有道理，恐惧确实会给出错误的建议。然后，我只需要提醒对方我察觉到他们处于恐惧之中。就这么简单，他们就会说："哦，好吧"，然后继续去做他们害怕做的事。当然，之后他们会回来对我说："马特，这太神奇了。太管用了。"

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: I mean, I'll give you examples. The most extreme is when a CEO realizes that there's a problem in the business and they haven't told their board yet and their board doesn't know, and remember, their board is their investors, and they have another round coming up, they know they're going to have to raise money in another six to 12 months. They need their current investors to participate in the upcoming round, otherwise outside investors won't. Then they say, well, what the hell do I do? I've got this problem. Do I tell my investors? And most often, the knee jerk reaction is, no, I'm not going to tell them.
turns.zh: 我举个最极端的例子。当一位首席执行官意识到公司存在问题，但还没告诉董事会，而董事会又不知道——记住，董事会就是投资者——而且他们即将进行下一轮融资，知道六到十二个月后必须筹集资金，需要现有投资者参与，否则外部投资者就不会加入。他们会说："天啊，我该怎么办？我遇到了这个问题。要不要告诉投资者？"大多数时候，第一反应是：不，我不能告诉他们。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Then I say, "Well, I think that's fear. I think if you actually tell them, tell your investors, the exact opposite of what we think is going to happen is going to happen. You think you're going to lose their trust. I think you're going to gain their trust." And so, if we've done this fear exercise before, they do it, they share transparently with their board all the problems and say, and I'm excited to tackle these problems. Every single time that's happened, the board members have said, "This is fantastic. I love this honesty. Thank you so much. This is one of the only companies that I'm on the board of that actually is transparent and honest," and they gain trust.
turns.zh: 然后我说："嗯，我觉得这就是恐惧。我认为如果你真的告诉他们，告诉你的投资者，事情会完全出乎你的预料。你以为会失去他们的信任，但实际上会赢得他们的信任。"如果我们之前做过这个恐惧练习，他们就会照做，向董事会透明地分享所有问题，说："我很兴奋能解决这些问题。"每次这样做后，董事会成员都会说："太棒了。我喜欢这种坦诚。太感谢你了。这是我所任职的唯一一家真正透明、诚实的公司。"于是他们赢得了信任。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm glad that you brought this topic up. I wanted to spend time on it. Just to double click a little bit into it, just kind of to summarize your advice here, if you feel fear, which you may not recognize you feel, the advice is: do the opposite of what your brain is telling you to do, right?
turns.zh: 很高兴你提到了这个话题。我想多花点时间深入探讨一下。简单总结一下你的建议，如果你感到恐惧——你可能没有意识到自己在恐惧——建议是：做大脑告诉你相反的事，对吧？

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Generally, I mean, check with someone. Don't just randomly, I feel fear crossing the street crossing a crowded highway and then go, oh, that's fear talking. I should cross the highway anyway and then get hit by a cop. No, that's not what I mean. I don't mean physical danger, I mean things that we perceive to be danger to our egos, but that the easiest thing is just to check with somebody else who's not in fear because they will be able to see clearly when you can't.
turns.zh: 通常，我是说，先去确认一下别人的意见。别随意乱来。我害怕过马路——尤其是拥堵的高速公路——然后就想，哦，这就是恐惧在作祟。但我还是应该过马路，然后可能被警察拦住。不，我不是这个意思。我说的不是身体上的危险，而是指我们认为会威胁到自我尊严的恐惧感。但最简单的方法就是找一个没有恐惧感的人确认一下，因为他们能在我们看不清的时候看得清。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was working through your curriculum and you pointed out that you found a way to express to somebody that they are in fear. I think it was your wife that kind of iterated on how to give you feedback that you're in fear where you didn't get defensive, you got more fearful and angry and can you talk a bit about that?
turns.zh: 我在学习你们的课程时，你们提到找到了一个方法，让别人知道他们处于恐惧状态。我记得是你的妻子教给你如何反馈对方处于恐惧状态，而你不会因此产生防御心理，反而会更加愤怒和生气。你能谈谈这方面吗？

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Yeah, so we iterated, I at times feel anger and I act on that anger and I don't even realize I'm in anger, so I wanted her to let me know, and so she would say, at first she said, "You're in anger," and that just made me feel accused and made me go into more anger. And then she said, "Are you in anger?" And that felt passive aggressive or indirect and that also made me go into more anger. Then finally she said, "I perceive you to be an anger." So it's an I statement and it's simply what she's perceiving. There's no judgment. That was able to punch through my anger and then I woke up and went, oh, and then I stopped and just didn't act until I was able to shift out of anger.
turns.zh: 是的。我们反复尝试过。我有时会感到愤怒，然后会被愤怒所驱使，甚至没有意识到自己处于愤怒状态。所以我希望她能让我知道，而她一开始会说，“你现在很生气。”这让我觉得被指责，更加愤怒。然后她会问，“你现在生气了吗？”这感觉带有消极攻击性或间接指责，也让我更加愤怒。最后她会说，“我察觉到你现在处于愤怒状态。”这是一个陈述事实的表述，只是她所感知到的。没有任何评判。这能穿透我的愤怒情绪，然后我清醒过来，停下来，直到能够摆脱愤怒情绪。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And anger and fear, I think there's different pieces of advice for if you feel angry versus fear. Is that right?
turns.zh: 太棒了。对于愤怒和恐惧，我想如果感觉到愤怒和恐惧，可能会有不同的建议。对吗？

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Yes. I mean, anger, you're just destroying and what you're doing is you're destroying relationships and so you just got to stop because you're breaking glass. Of course, you're breaking it with the people who are closest to you. They're the people who are nearest to you, which are the people you love and care about the most. They're not only people you work with, but they're the people you live with and you don't want to do that. You don't want to hurt them.
turns.zh: 是的。我的意思是，愤怒只会带来破坏，你会破坏人际关系。所以你必须停止这种行为，因为你在打破玻璃。当然，你打破的是与你最亲近的人的关系。他们是最亲近你的人，也是你最爱和最关心的人。他们不仅是同事，更是你的家人。你不想伤害他们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Maybe one last question along these lines, why do we do this? Is this just we're trying to protect our ego and ourselves and we just want to do the safe thing?
turns.zh: 是的。或许最后再问一个相关的问题，为什么我们会这样做？是因为我们想保护自己的自尊和自我吗？

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: That's it. I mean, I just learned very recently, and this isn't written anywhere because I just learned it, someone shared with me that anger is not a base emotion. Anger is actually a cover. It's a cover for when we feel pain, and so our brain doesn't want to feel the pain, so instead it externalizes it. But the problem is it shoves that pain onto everybody else around us. The real answer here is not to have people let us know that we're in anger and then stop. The real answer is just to allow ourselves to feel the pain and it sucks by the way, it actually hurts. But then we're not... Sorry, I'm getting emotional. We're not pushing that out onto other people and I only learned this very recently and I'm just starting to practice this and I'm still not good at it, but I'm now at least sometimes not going to anger.
turns.zh: 就是这样。我最近才意识到，这一点没写在任何地方，因为我刚刚才领悟到。有人告诉我，愤怒不是一种基本情绪。愤怒实际上是一种掩饰。当我们感到痛苦时，大脑不想直接面对痛苦，所以就把痛苦外化了。但问题是，这种痛苦会转嫁到我们身边的每个人身上。真正的解决之道不是让别人告诉我们我们处于愤怒状态然后停下来。真正的解决之道是允许自己感受痛苦，顺便说一句，这真的很痛苦。但这样我们就不会……抱歉，我情绪有点激动了。我们就不会把痛苦推给其他人了。我最近才意识到这一点，并且刚刚开始实践，但我现在至少有时不会陷入愤怒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting how personal this advice is that it sounds like something that you deal with. It's not just like you're this coach that's just like, hey guys, here's all these problems you have. Here's how you fix stuff that you help yourself with.
turns.zh: 真有趣的是，这些建议太贴近个人生活了，感觉就像在说你自己的经历。不是那种高高在上的教练式说教，告诉别人应该怎么做，而是实实在在的建议，让人觉得亲切易懂。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: I'm human. Yes, and that's why I try to figure it out with me and if I can figure something out with me, then I can share it with others.
turns.zh: 我也是普通人。没错，这就是为什么我会努力从自身出发去思考问题。如果我能从自身找到解决方案，就能把它分享给其他人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. That was a fruitful question from Leo, and we might come back to this topic.
turns.zh: 太棒了。利奥提出了一个很有价值的问题，我们或许会再回过头来讨论这个话题。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: By the way, this also applies to organizations. I mean, the way that I used to get all this information about how to run organizations is I started a company, Totality, and my co-founder and I, we did a terrible job running that company. What happened was I didn't have any learnings from that which I could share with people because it was just worst practices, not best practices. But then 10 years later, I thought to myself, well, how could I have done that better? How could we have done that better?
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，这同样适用于组织管理。举个例子，我创办Totality公司时，自己和合伙人把公司经营得一团糟。当时我从中汲取不到任何有用的经验教训，因为那些都是失败的案例，而不是成功的典范。但十年后，我突然意识到：我当时本可以做得更好啊！我们本可以把事情处理得更出色啊！

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: So, I picked up a book, a business book, it was High Output Management by Andy Grove. I read it and I was like, "Oh my God, here are all the answers." And then I read another book, The Hard Thing About Hard Things by Ben Horowitz was like, "Oh my God, there are even more answers." I just kept reading more and more business books, and every one I read, they were just chock full of answers. But then I needed to test whether or not these really worked, so that's when I started coaching and I started testing them in companies, but I had to let the people know here, do this, but they weren't going to read a 350 page book. I had to summarize it in two pages and then share it with them, and then they did, and then they implemented it and it worked.
turns.zh: 于是我拿起一本商业书籍——安迪·格鲁夫的《高效能人士的七个习惯》。我读完后惊呼：“天哪，所有问题的答案都在这里！”接着我又读了本·霍洛维茨的《最难的事》，心想：“哇塞，答案更多了！” 我不断研读商业书籍，每本都充满了宝贵的经验。但要验证这些方法是否有效，我必须亲自实践。于是我开始做教练，带着企业家们一起验证这些方法。但我得让他们明白：去试试这个方法吧！可他们根本不愿意通读350页的书籍。我必须把精华浓缩成两页，然后分享给他们。结果他们真的照做了，而且效果显著。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Then I had all these summaries, and then I started to create my own summaries of little niche cases that weren't in any book that I'd read. That's where all these writings came from. Then one day, someone that I was coaching said, "Matt, you got to take all these writings. They're a book, you got to publish them." And I said, "No, I don't." My friend said, "Well, how about I do all the work? How about I take care of the editing and the publishing?" And I was like, "Okay, if you want to do that, great." That was Alex MacCaw. Others had offered before, but he was the one that actually followed through all the way to the end. That was it. That's how the book was born.
turns.zh: 后来我积累了大量总结案例，发现很多案例书里都没写到。这就是我写作的源泉。有一天，我指导的一位客户说：“马特，你得把这些总结整理成书出版啊。”我说：“不，我不打算出版。”朋友说：“那让我来负责编辑和出版工作吧。”我说：“好啊，如果你愿意做，那太棒了。”这就是亚历克斯·麦考。其他人也曾提议过，但只有他坚持到底。就这样，这本书诞生了。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: But I realized also, recently, that many of my most radical ideas, I can't get anyone to test them because I'll say, "Hey, I think you should do blank." And the CEO will say, "That sounds crazy. Matt, can you point me to other examples of other people that have done this and it's worked?" And I say, "No, this is an original thought that came out of my head. No one's done it before that I know of." They're like, "Okay, well I'm not going to be the first."
turns.zh: 但最近我意识到，很多我最激进的想法都无法找到验证者，因为我会说：“嘿，我觉得你应该这么做。”CEO就会说：“这听起来太疯狂了。马特，能不能给我举个成功案例？”我说：“不行，这是我独创的想法，我知道之前没人这么做过。”对方就会说：“好吧，那我可不想当第一个吃螃蟹的人。”

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Then I realized I needed an organization to test my most radical ideas, and also all of my CEOs had been asking me to create software because I have a methodology and it's step one, step two, step three, and you do it in one-on-ones and then a methodology for a team meeting and then a methodology for feedback and then a methodology for every different motion in the company. It's all in Google Docs. And they said to me, "Matt, this is amazing. I love this one-on-one process. I love your team process, but I don't want to have to teach each of my reports the way you've taught me. I'd like it just being softer. I just hit a button and boom, it happens automatically." At first, I said, "No, that's not interesting to me. I'm not a developer. You, Brian Armstrong, you're a developer and you have a thousand engineers that work for you. Why don't you go create it?"
turns.zh: 然后我意识到，我需要一个组织来测试我最激进的想法。此外，我所有的CEO都一直要求我开发软件，因为我有一种方法论：第一步、第二步、第三步，分别用于一对一指导、团队会议、反馈收集，以及公司内各种决策流程。所有这些步骤都记录在Google Docs里。他们对我说：“马特，这太棒了。我喜欢这种一对一指导流程，也喜欢你的团队管理模式，但我不想让我手下每个下属都像你教我的那样去学习。我希望能更简单些。只要按个按钮，自动生成流程就行。”起初我说：“不行，这对我没什么吸引力。我又不是开发者。你，布莱恩·阿姆斯特朗，你才是开发者，而且你手下有上千名工程师。为什么不自己去开发呢？”

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: But in the end, I said, "Okay, this could be fun." So, I hired a team of developers and we started to create the software, and one, the product is working. But two more importantly, I now have a team of humans that we work together that I can start testing my more radical ideas out with. I would say about half of them are wildly successful and the other half complete duds. It almost seems like one are the other. But now I have my own basically laboratory to test things. Of course, when I see radical things that other people are doing, I try them in our organization, and it's phenomenal.
turns.zh: 但最后我还是说：“好吧，这挺有意思的。”于是我组建了一个开发团队，开始着手开发软件。首先，产品确实能正常运行。但更重要的是，现在我有了可以共同测试我更激进想法的团队成员。可以说，大约一半的想法取得了巨大成功，另一半则完全失败。两者似乎势不两立。但现在我有了自己的实验室来验证各种想法。当然，当我看到别人正在做的激进事物时，我也会在我们公司尝试，效果非常显著。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: I'll tell you the most radical one. I was asking one CEO, I said, "Have you ever let someone go and regretted it?" He said, "No." And I said, "Well, then you don't know what the bar is because the bar of where you should be letting people go is here, and the bar that you've let people go is here. So until you get close to that line, you don't know what that line is." He said, "Wow, that's true." Then I thought about it and I thought to myself, uh-oh, I have never let anyone go that I regret it, so I don't know where the line is.
turns.zh: 我要讲最激进的那个例子。我问一位CEO：“你有没有解雇过员工后又后悔的经历？”他说：“没有。”我说：“那你根本不知道标准线在哪里，因为你应该解雇员工的标准线在这里，实际解雇的标准线在这里。所以在你接近那条线之前，你根本不知道标准线在哪里。”他说：“哇，确实如此。”然后我仔细一想，糟糕，我从未解雇过后又后悔的人，所以我也不知道标准线在哪里。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Then I thought, oh no, I've got to go into my team and let someone go, and here's the problem. We've already done talent density, we've already done the Netflix thing. If someone is meeting expectation, we let them go. We've already let all those folks go. So on our team, it's only outperformers. So, I thought there was one guy, he's an outperformer, no question about it, and super positive, an amazing guy and can do anything and is happy to do everything. But there wasn't much left for him to do because everything else was being covered. I talked to my number two and said, "Can you do what you're doing and what he's doing?" And she said, "Give me two weeks," and she did. She came back and said, "Yeah, I can." So, we let him go.
turns.zh: 接着我又想，天哪，我得去我的团队里解雇人，问题是。我们已经做了人才密度分析，也实施了Netflix的做法。如果员工达到预期标准，我们就解雇他们。我们已经解雇了所有那些人。所以在我们团队里，全是表现超出预期的人。我想到了一个人，毫无疑问他表现出色，积极向上，能力超群，乐于承担任何任务。但他已经没有太多事情可做了，因为其他工作都被分担了。我和我的二号人物说：“你能接手你现在做的工作和他现在做的工作吗？”她说：“给我两周时间。”结果她成功了。她回来后说：“是的，我能做到。”于是我们解雇了他。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Now, when I let someone go, I try to do it with a massive amount of compassion because I know it's brutal. I mean, losing your spouse, your home, and your job, these are the three most traumatic things that can happen to you. When that happens, of course you go into massive fear and the brain shuts down, so I want to be there and help them through that process and actively help them find their dream job because there is a place that absolutely needs them. So, what I do is I become their agent and I say, "I want to help you discover what it is that your ideal role is, and I want to help you create it or land it." I did that with him. Turns out, what he wanted to do was go start a company and create a new product so he could just start that day one. But, the litmus for me is that everybody I've let go, I believe anyway, that I continue to be friends with. That shows me that the process by which I let people go is a humane one.
turns.zh: 如今，当我让某人离职时，我会尽可能怀着同理心去做这件事，因为我深知这份离别之痛。失去配偶、失去家园、失去工作——这些是人生最沉重的打击。面对这些变故，人难免陷入恐惧，思维也会陷入停滞。因此，我想陪伴他们走过这个过程，主动帮他们寻找理想的工作机会，因为总有地方在等着他们。为此，我会充当他们的代理人，对他们说："我想帮你找到理想的职位，并助你达成目标。"我对那位男士就是这么做的。结果发现，他最想做的是创办公司、开发新产品，第二天就能从零开始。但对我来说，最重要的衡量标准是，每个被我裁掉的人，我都保持着友谊。这让我确信，我裁员的方式是人性化的。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Here's the crazy thing, after letting this guy go, after about 30 days, I was like, ugh, did I do the wrong thing? Was that too much? But then after about two to three months, I realized, no, that actually was the right thing because my number two was able to absorb the things that he was doing and here's the crazy part, with fewer people in the organization, things work better. That's the big realization that most people never discover. they hit product market fit, they get tons of money from investors, just higher, higher, higher, higher, but every additional human you have in your organization causes extra overhead and geometrically so, because now you have to keep all those people informed, give them all context, make them all feel heard, because unless they feel like they're contributing and you understand what they're saying, then they feel ignored and they feel passed over and they feel disrespected and grumpy.
turns.zh: 最疯狂的是，让那个人离职后约30天，我会想，天哪，我做错了吗？是不是太过分了？但两三个月后，我意识到，不，我做的是正确的决定。因为我的二号人物接手了他的工作，关键是，随着团队规模缩小，工作效率反而更高了。这是大多数人从未意识到的深刻真相。他们实现了产品与市场的契合，获得了投资者的巨额资金，一路高歌猛进。但每增加一个员工，都会带来指数级增长的管理成本——因为你得向所有人通报情况、解释背景、确保每个人被倾听。除非他们感受到自己的贡献，理解你的意图，否则他们会感到被忽视、被忽略、被不尊重、脾气暴躁。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: There's this morale problem that exists. There's this friction of information flow and a morale problem that grows and grows and grows. Really, the only answer is, I mean, that's why people bring me in because they're growing, growing, growing, and things are breaking. I have a system that keeps things together, but it doesn't make it perfect. It just makes it so that the company doesn't fall apart. But really the ideal is just to keep the team super small. That's what WhatsApp did, that's what Instagram did, that's what Linear is doing right now. That's what Notion has been doing for a while. Those, to me, are the real success stories.
turns.zh: 这种士气问题由来已久。信息流通的摩擦和士气问题的恶性循环不断加剧。唯一的解决之道是——这也是人们请我介入的原因——在增长过程中，及时修补裂痕。我有套能维系团队的系统，但它并非完美之选，只是防止公司崩盘。但理想的状态是保持团队极小规模。这正是WhatsApp、Instagram、Linear和Notion成功的秘诀。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This reminds me of a story I just listened to on Lex Fridman's podcast. They were interviewing the head of AI at Tesla, or former head of AI, and Lex was asking him, "Why did you get rid of LiDAR on your cars? Like aren't more sensors good so that you can be better at self-driving?" And he's like, "If you have LiDAR, you got to think about the supply chain and getting all those parts. You got to think about all the additional data that it brings and adds more chaos to your data, and you have to think about that. Think about if that one part is gone, everything slows down, and in theory it is better, but then all these other factors end up making it worse." Talking about how Elon's philosophy is the best part is no part. It feels like that's exactly what you're saying.
turns.zh: 这让我想起最近在Lex Fridman播客上听到的故事。他们采访特斯拉人工智能部门主管，或者说前主管，Lex问他："为什么你们的汽车取消激光雷达？多传感器不是能提升自动驾驶能力吗？"他回答："如果用激光雷达，你得考虑供应链、零部件采购，处理额外数据会增加系统复杂度，万一某个零部件故障，整个系统就会陷入停滞。理论上多传感器更好，但实际因素却适得其反。"这让我联想到埃隆的理念："少即是多"。感觉你说的道理如出一辙。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're getting to all the stuff I want to talk about, which is awesome. So firing people, this is good. We were chatting earlier and you mentioned that this is a skill that most managers are really bad at and maybe is the most important skill to develop as a leader and as a manager. People are just bad at it. You shared a few pieces of advice there, but is there anything else that you could share about just how to get better at firing people and that skill?
turns.zh: 你提到了我最想聊的所有话题，这太棒了。所以说解雇员工这事儿做得好，真是难能可贵。我们之前聊过，你提到这是大多数管理者最不擅长的技能，或许也是作为领导者和管理者最需要培养的核心能力。人们在这方面确实做得很糟糕。你之前分享了一些建议，但还有没有什么其他要点能帮助我们更好地掌握解雇员工的技巧和这项技能呢？

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Yeah, the reason people are bad at this is because they think that they're hurting the person who they're letting go. I mean, how many times have I heard from someone, "Yeah, this person's not performing, but gosh, they really need this job and their mother has cancer," and whatever personal situation they're in. Wei Deng, who is the CEO of Clipboard Health, who's one of my favorite CEOs, who frankly I learn more from her than she learns from me, she shared with me her framework for making decisions, which is she separates the decision from the implementation, meaning she thinks about who is the stakeholder here that I'm solving for? And almost always in a company, you're solving for the customer. So, what would the customer want to see happen? That's the decision. Of course, the customer would want to see only the best employees and anyone who isn't a great employee, don't be there.
turns.zh: 是啊，人之所以做不好这件事，是因为他们总觉得自己在伤害被裁员工。我听过太多人说：“是啊，这个人表现不佳，但天啊，他们真的很需要这份工作，况且他们母亲还在患癌”之类的话。还有各种个人困境。Clipboard Health的CEO韦登是我最欣赏的CEO之一，坦白说，我从她身上学到的东西比她从我这里得到的要多得多。她分享的决策框架是，将决策与执行分开。意思是，你要思考：我要为谁解决问题？在公司里通常都是为客户服务。所以，客户希望看到什么结果？这就是决策。当然，客户希望看到的是最优秀的员工，而不优秀的员工就应该离开。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Now the implementation is, if I do this, if I let this person go, who gets hurt? Well, the employee gets hurt. Maybe I get hurt because it's a painful conversation. Maybe the rest of the team gets hurt because they're sad that their friend is leaving. Then you look at, well, what can we do? Each person who gets hurt, what is it that they really want? Let's see if we can help them get what they really want. Well, the person let go, what do they want? They want a great job where they're actually needed and they feel fulfilled, so they enjoy what they're doing and they're actually critical to the company or organization that they're with. Right now they're not, by the way, they're not critical, clearly. So you're actually holding them back from what it is that they really want.
turns.zh: 现在说执行层面。如果我解雇这个人，谁会受到伤害？员工会受伤。可能我自己也会受伤，因为这是一次痛苦的谈话。团队其他人也会受伤，因为他们为朋友的离开感到难过。那么，怎么办呢？每个受伤的人真正想要什么？看看能否帮他们实现真正的愿望。被解雇的人想要什么？他们想要一份真正需要他们的工作，让自己感到充实，享受工作，并对所在公司或组织至关重要。显然，他们现在并不重要。所以你其实是在阻碍他们实现真正想要的。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: What you do is you help them find that place that really needs the skill or the passion that they have. Yourself, what do you really want? You want to not have a difficult conversation? Well, cognitive behavior therapy, the best way to get over that is to actually have one and realize it's not that bad. Then the rest of the team, they feel sad because their teammate left. Well, here's how you solve what they really want is they want to know that... They want to release their emotions. Okay, great. Listen to them, let them share their emotions, let them share the sadness that they feel, and then it's released out of their body.
turns.zh: 你要做的是帮他们找到真正需要他们的技能或激情的地方。你自己呢？你不想进行艰难的谈话？那认知行为疗法是最好的解决办法，就是亲自去谈一谈，然后发现其实没那么糟糕。至于团队其他人，他们因为同事离开而难过。你要做的就是帮他们释放情绪。好的，没问题。倾听他们，听他们分享情绪，听他们倾诉悲伤，然后这些情绪就会被释放出来。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Decision is one thing, implementation is completely and utterly separate. That's the same thing here in letting someone go. But if you let them go kindly and humanely, the key is, in my opinion, you become their agent, like Michael Ovitz, the CAA agent. You help them find their next job actively. Michael Ovitz is the one who reaches out to employers for his clients and says, "Hey, do you have work for my client?" That's what I mean by being agent, not by, if you need a reference from me, I'll be happy to give you reference. That's bullshit, that's passive.
turns.zh: 决策是一回事，执行则完全分开。在解雇员工这件事上也是如此。但如果你能友善、人性化地解雇员工，关键在于，在我看来，要成为他们的代理人，就像CAA经纪人迈克尔·奥维茨那样。主动帮他们寻找下一个工作机会。迈克尔·奥维茨会为客户联系雇主，说：“嘿，你有适合我客户的工作吗？”这才是成为代理人的意思，而不是说如果你需要我的推荐信，我很乐意提供。这就是被动的做法。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: I'm talking about active, and it doesn't take long. Maybe one to two hours of my time reaching out to people I know saying, "Hey, I've got this great person." Oh my God, of course they're going to pay attention. Of course, they're going to react. Now you might say, well, wait a second, what if the person isn't great? What if they're a bad performer and my posit is that they're good at something. You have to find out what it is they're good at. And really what they're good at is what they're passionate about, so find out what they're passionate about and that you can recommend them for. That's what I do.
turns.zh: 我说的是主动行动，而且这不需要花费太多时间。比如花一到两个小时联系我认识的人，说：“嘿，我发现了一个很棒的人。”天哪，他们肯定会关注的。他们肯定会做出回应的。你可能会问，等等，如果那个人不怎么样呢？如果他们表现不佳，而你却坚信他们擅长某项技能呢？你必须先发现他们擅长什么。其实他们擅长的，就是他们所热爱的，因此要找到他们的热情所在，并据此为他们推荐。这就是我的做法。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: I think for almost all managers that aren't good at letting go, it's because A, they've never done it, or B, they've done it badly. They didn't help the person, and that person then went off and had a very painful time and now hates that manager. But if you actively help that person, they will appreciate it. Now, there are situations when a person says, "Screw you, I don't want your help." Okay, but they still recognize that you offered.
turns.zh: 我认为对于那些不擅长放手的管理者来说，原因无非两点：A，他们从未尝试过；B，他们做得太糟糕。他们没有帮助到对方，结果那个人离开后经历了痛苦的时期，现在对那位管理者心怀怨恨。但如果你主动帮助他们，他们会心怀感激的。当然，有些情况下对方会说：“去你的吧，我不需要你的帮助。” 好吧，但他们至少会认可你的好意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Who's the best person at firing that comes to mind when you think of this person's really good at this?
turns.zh: 当你想到这个人真正擅长这件事时，谁是解雇方面最出色的人？

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Wei Deng from Clipboard Health. She's the most compassionate.
turns.zh: Clipboard Health的魏登。她是最富同理心的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. The framework you shared reminds me of something my manager once taught me similarly. They missed the final piece of actually being their agent and finding their next gig, but just the idea of separate the emotion and doing the thing from, if there were no feelings involved, what would you do? And then you should do that, and that might be hard.
turns.zh: 太棒了。你分享的这个框架让我想起我的经理曾教给我的类似理念。他们忽略了最后一步，即真正成为他们的代理人并为他们寻找下一个机会，但关键在于将情感与行动分开——如果没有情感牵绊，你会怎么做？然后你就应该照做，这可能很难。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: That's exactly right. By the way, this whole thing about no feelings, I do have probably two CEOs that don't feel emotions. They don't feel fear, they don't feel anger. One, in particular, feels zero emotions. I have to say, he's a machine, he's an operating machine and there's zero time between ah, this is the right thing to do and doing it. It's amazing. It's an incredibly well run company and an incredibly valuable company. So yeah, emotions typically, again, typically fear and anger are the ones that derail our brains.
turns.zh: 完全正确。顺便说一句，关于无情感这件事，我认识两个CEO，他们几乎没有情感。他们不感到恐惧，不感到愤怒。其中一位尤其毫无情感。我得说，他就是个机器，一个运作机器，从来没有从“这件事该做”到“去做”的延迟时间。真是令人惊叹。这是一家运营得极其出色、极具价值的公司。所以是的，情感通常——再说一次，通常恐惧和愤怒会让我们的大脑失控。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It makes me think of Alex Honnold, I think is his name, the free climber, the solo dude. His amygdala doesn't quite function so he doesn't-
turns.zh: 这让我想起亚历克斯·霍诺德，我想是这个名字，那个自由攀岩者，独自攀岩的人。他的大脑扁桃体不太正常，所以他——

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's interesting. He could be a free solo climber, he could be a CEO.
turns.zh: 真有趣。他既可以是自由攀岩者，也可以是CEO。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: That's right. CEO's a little safer. The prediction for Alex is that he will at some point, unfortunately die.
turns.zh: 没错。CEO的工作相对安全些。但亚历克斯的预估结果是，不幸的是，他最终会丧命。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Did you see The Alpinist? Not to spoil anything.
turns.zh: 是的。你看过《登山者》吗？我不想剧透。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 看过。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, moving on from that, I'm curious, in a remote world, does your advice change in terms of firing? It seems like everything you shared you could do easily in person or remote, but does something change when you're doing it over Zoom?
turns.zh: 好的，接下来我很好奇，在远程办公的环境下，解雇方面的建议是否会有所不同？看起来你分享的所有技巧，无论是面对面还是远程都能轻松完成，但通过Zoom进行时会有什么变化吗？

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: No, it doesn't change at all. There is one point I didn't include, which I'll include now, is there's helping the person be their agent, but there's also allowing the person, whenever I have a difficult conversation, I start it off, "Hey, this is going to be a difficult conversation. I want you to take a few seconds and prepare yourself. You are not going to enjoy this." What I found is that the way the amygdala gets triggered is often because of surprise. So, if you give someone just a few seconds to mentally prepare, then the amygdala often doesn't get triggered nearly as hard because if they're aware that they're going to go into fear, they're going to go into anger, they're going to go into sadness, then they can see it coming and they go, oh, that's what it is. But if they don't see it coming, just a surprise and all of a sudden it grips their whole brain and now they're in it and they don't even know they're in it.
turns.zh: 不会，一点儿也不会改变。还有一点我之前没提到，现在要补充一下，就是要让对方成为自己的代言人，但同时也要让他们做好心理准备。每当我要进行艰难对话时，我都会先说：“嘿，这次对话可能会有些困难。我希望你能花几秒钟时间做好心理准备。你可能不会喜欢这个过程。”我发现，当杏仁核被激活时，往往是因为意外。所以，如果你给对方几秒钟时间做好心理准备，杏仁核就不会那么强烈地被激活了。因为如果他们意识到自己即将陷入恐惧、愤怒或悲伤，他们就能预见这种情绪的到来，然后想：“哦，原来是这样。” 但如果他们毫无防备，突如其来的情绪就会完全占据他们的思维，让他们措手不及，甚至意识不到自己正在被情绪控制。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: That's the first thing I do. This is going to be a difficult conversation. Are you ready? Then I share the news. I'm letting you go, here's why. Then second, I deliver the message. The third thing is now they're feeling emotions, strong ones. Even though I warned them, they're still feeling them. Now you want them to be able to release those emotions, and so I say to them, "My guess is you're feeling a lot of anger right now, fear, sadness. Is that true? And if so, would you be willing to share with me what you're feeling and what you're thinking?" Sometimes they don't answer, but many times they do and they share with me and they let it out. That's important to allow them to let it out. Then I make them feel heard and I actively listen. That makes them realize that I'm not trying to run away from the pain that they're feeling. I'm not trying to leave them alone with it. I sit with them as they have it and then I try to help them get through it.
turns.zh: 这是我首先要做的。我会说：“这将是一次艰难的对话。你准备好了吗？” 然后我传达消息：“我要解雇你了，原因如下。” 接下来，我会表达我的关切：“你准备好了吗？” 然后我分享这个消息：“我要解雇你了，原因如下。” 接下来，我传达我的信息：“第三步，现在他们正在经历强烈的情绪。即使我提前警告过他们，他们还是会感受到这些情绪。现在你需要帮助他们释放这些情绪。所以我会问他们：‘我猜你现在正感到非常愤怒、恐惧、悲伤。对吗？如果是这样，你愿意和我分享你的感受和想法吗？’” 有时他们不回答，但很多时候他们会回答，然后和我分享他们的情绪。这很重要，要让他们能把情绪释放出来。 然后我让他们感受到被倾听，我会积极倾听。这能让他们意识到，我不是在逃避他们正在经历的痛苦。我不是要让他们独自面对这些痛苦。我会陪伴他们，帮助他们度过难关。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's something else I wanted to chat about is the feeling heard lesson that you have for people. I'd love to just get your advice on just how to help people feel heard. It's like, oh yeah, I know that's important. I want people to feel heard. I will listen and it'll go great. But you have some very tactical advice on how to actually make people feel heard.
turns.zh: 还有一点我想聊聊的，就是你给人们的被倾听的课程。我很想听听你的建议，如何真正让人们感受到被倾听。我会说：“哦，对，我知道这很重要。我希望人们能感受到被倾听。我会倾听，一切都会顺利。” 但你有一些非常实用的建议，如何真正让人们感受到被倾听。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Yeah, there's sort of a few different levels of it. One way to make people feel heard is, let's assume you're talking to them because there's another way, there's an even more surface way is verbal. Sometimes what I do is I ask, if I'm in a group of people, and there's a question or a problem that we're trying to solve, instead of going around the room and hearing people's verbal opinions, which takes forever, I ask everyone at the same time to take five minutes to write down their solution. Then we all drop it in a doc and then I just read it. When I read it I say, "Thank you, Lenny." And that makes you know that I at least read it, so that's a little bit of feeling heard.
turns.zh: 是的，有几种不同的方法。让人们感受到被倾听的一种方法是，假设你和他们交谈是因为还有另一种更表面化的方法，那就是口头表达。有时我的做法是，如果我在一群人中，遇到一个我们试图解决的问题或难题，而不是让每个人在房间里轮流表达他们的口头意见，这会花很长时间，我会让每个人同时花五分钟写下他们的解决方案。然后我们把它们都放进一个文档里，然后我读出来。读的时候我会说：“谢谢你，Lenny。” 这样你就知道我至少读过了，所以这就是一点被倾听的感觉。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Second, if I want to make you feel more heard, I ask you to say it verbally and then I repeat it back to you. "Lenny, I think what I heard you say is... Is that right?" And you're like, "Yes." Or you're like, "No, not quite a little bit different." Then if it's a little bit different, I repeat it again until you say, "Yes, that's it." Now you know that I understood you.
turns.zh: 第二，如果我想让你们更感受到被倾听，我会让你们口头说出来，然后我再重复一遍：“Lenny，我认为你说的是……对吗？”然后你会说：“对。” 或者你会说：“不，不太对，有点不同。” 如果确实有不同之处，我会再重复一遍，直到你说：“对，就是这样。” 现在你知道我理解你了。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Then there's a third way which is even deeper, which is especially if you're giving me feedback, you likely don't want to hurt my feelings. So what you're doing is you're giving me the feedback, but you're couching it, you're polishing it, you're rounding the edges, you're making it softer. It's not really what you're thinking, but it's what you're willing to say. If I want to make you really feel heard, I reflect back what I imagine are the thoughts in your head. If I think you're feeling anger, I sort of think to myself, well, what would anger feel like? I cause myself to feel that anger, then what are the thoughts that appear to me? I say something to you like, "Lenny, I think what I'm hearing you say is you're off and you're thinking, screw you, Matt. How dare you walk into the office and not even say hello to me? Is that close?" And you're like, "No, Matt."
turns.zh: 还有第三种更深入的方法，特别是当你给我反馈时，你可能不想伤害我的感情。所以你做的是把反馈委婉表达、润色修饰、去尖锐化，让它更温和。这不是你真实的想法，而是你愿意说出口的话。如果我想让你真正感受到被倾听，我会反馈给你我想象中你脑中的想法。比如，如果我觉得你很生气，我会想，生气会是什么感觉？我会让自己感受到那种愤怒，然后看看脑中浮现的想法。我会对你说：“莱尼，我觉得你现在很生气，还在想，‘去你的，马特。你怎么敢走进办公室连招呼都不打一个？’”你可能会说：“不，马特。”

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: People either say one of two things, they say, "Yeah, that is it." Or they say "No, that's stronger than what I was thinking, but directionally that's right." What that really means is, yeah, that's what I was thinking. Almost always their thoughts are bigger than their words, but they really feel heard when I share their thoughts. Now, that's not the end of the process. I mean you actually have to then do something. Once you made them feel heard, you have to say, okay, well either I accept or don't accept this feedback and if I accept, here's what I'm going to do about it. If I don't accept, I need to explain to you why. Here's what's going on. You shared with me what's going on in your world, now let me share with you what's going on in my world. Hopefully, you can see why this thing that's going on in my world doesn't allow me to accept what it is that you shared, and hopefully now that you see what's going on in my world, your feedback changes and that's it. That's the whole process.
turns.zh: 人们通常会说两种话，一种是“对，就是这样。”另一种是“不，这比我想象的更有力，但方向是对的。”这其实意味着，“对，就是我这么想的。” 人们的想法往往比他们说出来的更丰富，但当我分享他们的想法时，他们会感觉被倾听了。不过这还不是整个过程的结束。接下来你必须采取行动。一旦让他们感受到被倾听，你就得说，是的，我接受还是不接受这个反馈。如果接受，就说我要怎么做。如果不接受，就要解释原因，说明情况。你分享了你世界里的情况，现在让我分享我世界里的情况吧。希望你能明白为什么我世界里的情况不允许我接受你的反馈，希望现在你能理解我世界里的情况后，你的反馈会改变，整个过程就完成了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm listening to this advice and I'm like, yes, I will do this next time I'm talking to someone. I imagine people don't and they forget, and it takes time to actually learn these things. Like the firing advice you just shared, how do you actually get good at this and practice these things is like I have to work with a coach who will continue to reinforce these things? Is it follow these steps next time? Have them written down? What advice do you have for folks that are like, I want to get better at this. I want to start doing this stuff.
turns.zh: 我听了这些建议，觉得是的，我下次和别人交流时会这么做。我想人们可能不会这样做，他们会忘记，而真正学会这些需要时间。比如你刚刚分享的解雇建议，如何真正擅长这件事并加以练习？是不是需要和教练一起练习？下次照步骤做？把步骤写下来？对于那些想提高自己的人，你有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Well, these docs are all free to the public in the curriculum. You can post them here, you can post them on Twitter, you can post the whole curriculum on Twitter, frankly, other people have. It has a step-by-step. There's a doc in there that is a step-by-step script. All you do is you read it and you follow the script in letting someone go or in making someone feel heard. My posit is once you do it one time, you're like, oh my god, that worked so well. That's the only motivation you need. And you've got the script, so you can just keep doing it. I don't think you need a coach.
turns.zh: 嗯，这些文档在课程中都是免费公开的。你可以在这里发布，也可以在推特上发布，甚至整个课程都可以发布在推特上，其他人已经这么做了。里面有分步指南。有一份文档是分步脚本。你只需要阅读并按照脚本行事，让别人离开或让他们感觉被倾听。我的观点是，一旦你做过一次，你就会说，天哪，这太有效了。这就是你唯一需要的动力。你有脚本了，所以可以一直这么做。我觉得你不需要教练。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: In fact, I remember one time I asked an investor who their best up and coming CEO was. The investor gave me a name. I was like, "Great, can I please get introduced to him? I want coach him." I reached out, the guy responded immediately. He's like, "Matt, I've read your book. I love your book. I read it three years ago. I've been implementing all the elements in our company. It's fantastic." When someone says that they know my work, they've already implemented it and it's worked, 10 out of 10 times, that person wants me to coach them. Then I said, "Great, that's fantastic. I'd love to coach you." And the guy said to me, "No, thanks." I was shocked. I was like, "Why?" He said, "Well, because it's all working. I don't have any problems. I don't think I need to be coached by you." I couldn't have heard a better answer. That, to me, is the ultimate answer. And he is right. He doesn't need me, doesn't need anyone.
turns.zh: 事实上，我记得有一次我问一位投资者，他们最看好的新晋CEO是谁。投资者给了我一个名字。我当时就说，“太棒了，能帮我介绍一下吗？我想指导他。”我联系了那个人，他立刻回复了。他说：“马特，我读过你的书。我很喜欢你的书。三年前我就读过，现在我们公司一直在践行书中的所有理念，效果棒极了。” 当有人说他们了解我的作品，并且已经成功应用且效果显著时，他们通常会希望我来指导他们。然后我说：“太好了，我很乐意指导你。”那个人却说：“不了，谢谢。”我很震惊，问：“为什么？”他回答：“因为一切都很顺利。我没有任何问题。觉得不需要你来指导。” 这简直是最完美的回答。在我看来，这就是终极答案。他说得没错，他不需要我，也不需要任何人。

turns.zh: 我差点想问，这么多年写作和体系化建设的目的，难道就是为了让自己变得可有可无吗？
