turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That actually reminds me of another question a reader asked on Twitter who happened to be the one on only Ryan Hoover. He asked, "How has your approach changed in your coaching since you started?"
turns.zh: 这让我想起推特上一位读者的问题，碰巧他就是Ryan Hoover。读者问：“自从你开始做教练以来，你的方法有何变化？”

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Ryan obviously started Product Hunt and then he sold the company to AngelList, so he was part of AngelList when I went there because I was coaching Naval. What we realized coaching Naval is that Naval did not want to be CEO and he just didn't know how to get out. So, I said there's a way and I can show you, and so I did and made Naval's life 10 times better. Frankly, made AngelList 10 times better because Naval wasn't enjoying being CEO, therefore he wasn't good at it. We ended up putting someone in who did a fine job, then put someone else in who's doing an insanely good job. Now, of course, AngelList is massively valuable.
turns.zh: Ryan显然创立了Product Hunt，随后将公司出售给AngelList。所以我去AngelList指导Naval时，他还是AngelList的成员。我们发现Naval并不想当CEO，只是不知道如何摆脱这个角色。于是我说有办法，我可以教你，后来我确实做到了，让Naval的生活好了十倍。坦白说，也让AngelList好了十倍，因为Naval不享受CEO的角色，所以表现不佳。最终我们换了合适的人选，现在换了更出色的人选。如今，AngelList价值巨高。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Ryan was there at the time, Ryan Hoover, great guy, I love Ryan. So, what has changed since then? I think what's changed is I don't think back then I had any of this fear and anger give bad advice. I think back then it was all very tactical. It was all very high up management type stuff, which is you need to have goals and at the company level, at the department level, at the individual level, you then need to track those goals. You need to track all the agreements that people make, all the actions they say they'll do. You have to put it all in Asana. Everyone has to be able to see each other's Asana board so they can see what each other is doing. I still do that, but now I've added on this piece of oh, you're in the moment and you're feeling fear? Okay, you still got to go forward. That's sort of the big change.
turns.zh: 瑞安当时也在场，瑞安·胡佛，真是个很棒的人，我很喜欢瑞安。那么，从那以后有什么变化呢？我认为最大的变化在于，我那时并没有任何恐惧和愤怒情绪，也不会给出错误建议。我觉得那时一切都非常务实。都是高层管理层面的事情——你需要设定目标，无论是公司层面、部门层面还是个人层面，然后追踪这些目标，追踪人们达成的所有协议和承诺的行动。这些都需要录入Asana系统。每个人都必须能看到彼此的Asana任务板，这样才能了解彼此的进展。我现在还是会这么做，但现在我又增加了一个环节：当你身处当下，感受到恐惧和愤怒时，该怎么办？好吧，你还是得继续前进。这才是最大的变化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I noticed that's at the top of the curriculum. Do you find that's where a lot of the biggest transformations happen, that curriculum component?
turns.zh: 我注意到这部分内容在课程顶部。你觉得这个课程模块是发生最大变革的地方吗？

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Absolutely. I cause people when they first start coaching, they have to read that first. There's sort of three seminal documents: on time, top goal, and fear and anger give bad advice. On time just says, hey, we're going to start our meetings on time and you're going to show up and if you don't show up on time, you're going to let me know first. That's just because I don't want to... And by the way, I showed up two minutes late for us. That's because I was on the Google Hangout for 10 minutes. I didn't realize, I thought you were-
turns.zh: 绝对是的。刚开始指导别人时，他们必须先读这部分内容。主要有三个关键文档：按时开始、顶级目标，以及恐惧和愤怒会导致错误建议。按时开始就是说，嘿，我们的会议要准时开始，你要按时到场。如果你不按时到场，就得先告知我。这只是因为我不想……顺便说一句，我那次开会就迟到了两分钟，因为我在Google环聊上待了10分钟。我没意识到，还以为你们在等我——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm trying to fix that bug. Every time we send an invite, there's a Google meet button there. I think I cracked it finally. Yeah, that would've been a funny podcast where I'm just sitting here starting on time and for two minutes. Hello, we're just waiting.
turns.zh: 我正在修复这个漏洞。每次发送邀请时，都会有一个Google Meet按钮。我终于搞定了。要是那次播客我能准时开始，坐在那儿等两分钟，那该多有趣啊。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Exactly. Second one is top goal, which is this concept from McKeown, who wrote Essentialism, which is everyone is making requests of you, but if all you do is spend all day is responding to other people's requests, you never actually march towards your own priorities. You need to A, create priorities and then set aside some amount of time each day, 30 minutes, an hour, two hours that you just work on your own priority. If you do that, you'll make massive gains. And that's true. I mean, in five minutes I can change someone's life just by having them follow that practice. Then the third one is, if you're in anger, give that advice and that's what I have people read and say, "Does this resonate with you?" If it does, we can work together and if it doesn't, we shouldn't work together. So yeah, that's kind of like the crux document of whether or not people philosophically are going to resonate with what I have to share.
turns.zh: 第二个是顶级目标，这是麦基翁（McKeown）在《精要主义》中提出的概念。别人总是向你提出要求，但如果你整天都在回应别人的请求，就永远无法朝着自己的优先事项前进。你需要A、设定优先事项，然后每天留出30分钟、一小时或两小时专门处理自己的优先事项。如果你能做到，就会取得巨大进步。确实如此。比如五分钟内，我只要让别人遵循这个做法，就能改变他们的生活。第三个是，当你处于愤怒情绪中时，别给出建议。这是我让大家阅读并问“这点你能共鸣吗？”如果能共鸣，我们就能合作；如果不能，就不合作。所以说，这三个文档是衡量人们在理念上是否与我产生共鸣的核心文件。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The top goal piece, I'm reading a book called Make Time right now and that's a big part of it. I actually just added top goal to my calendar every day. It's not working yet. Every time I get to it, I'm like no, I'm going to just check Twitter right now. But I'm working on it.
turns.zh: 关于顶级目标这部分，我现在正在读一本叫《掌控时间》的书，这也是其中的核心内容。我刚把顶级目标添加到日历里，但暂时还没效果。每次要执行时，总会想：不，先去看看推特吧。但我正在努力改进。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: That is the hardest part. Now, what I've done is I'm similar. During my top goal time, I have somebody sit with me and they prevent me from doing anything but my top goal.
turns.zh: 这确实是最难的部分。现在我采取了类似做法。在执行顶级目标的时间段里，有人陪着我，防止我做任何与顶级目标无关的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wait, can you talk a bit more about that? Is this like a coworker? Are you just like, "I need you here for this hour every day?"
turns.zh: 等等，你能再详细说说吗？这就像同事之间的关系吗？你是不是就只是说，“你每天需要在这里待一个小时”？

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Yeah, I mean it's like the same idea as a trainer in a gym. A trainer in a gym, maybe they're teaching you a little bit, but more often than not they're just forcing you to do the thing that you know need to do. But if they weren't there, you would kind of go eh and not do it. That's all this is. It's what I call an accountability partner.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得这和健身房里的教练是一个道理。健身房的教练，可能也会指导你一点，但更多时候他们只是逼你去做那些你明明知道需要做却不爱做的事。比如开会，我可以开20次会，甚至连续开10小时的会，都没问题——尤其是当我是主讲人、是主动参与者的时候。但做异步任务对我来说太难了，因为我太以人为中心了。如果没有其他人在身边，我就很难坚持下去，所以我需要另一个人陪着我。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: There's even an app now where you can go online and you can sign up and I think it costs like $5 a month and you can sign up to meet someone else and you become accountability partners to each other. It's insanely effective. I'm not the only one that has a problem focusing on tasks that I don't love that are necessary, but I don't love. Like a meeting, I could take a meeting, I could take 20 meetings, I could take 10 hours of meetings, no problem. Especially when I'm the presenter, when I'm the active one. But doing asynchronous tasks for me because so people-oriented that when there isn't another human with me, it's painful, so I just have another human with me.
turns.zh: 这太棒了。而且那个人可能在做其他工作，我想他们不会全天盯着你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. And that person is doing other work, I imagine they're not just watching you full-time.
turns.zh: 不，他们可以做自己想做的事。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: No, they can do whatever they want.
turns.zh: 你是在向领导者和CEO们推荐这种方法吗？就是让某个人在那里待一个小时。哇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is this what you recommend to leaders and CEOs? Just have someone there for an hour. Wow.
turns.zh: 如果你的性格和我一样，那没错，就找个人在那里。可以远程办公，也可以面对面交流，都不重要。但面对面更有效。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: If your personality is like mine, yes, have someone there. It can be remote, it can be in person, it doesn't matter. In person's a little bit more effective.
turns.zh: 对，应该有个小Zoom窗口。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right, there's like a little zoom window.
turns.zh: 我让我的孩子们这么做。他们很喜欢。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: I have my kids do it. They love it.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个功能。我用的一个叫Centered的应用，我是它的投资者，但我一直都在用，他们还有一个Buddy功能，可以实时匹配搭档。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. There's an app I use called Centered, that app that I'm an investor in, but I use it all the time and they have this buddy feature actually where you can be paired with a buddy in real time.
turns.zh: 对，对。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Yes, yes.
turns.zh: 是的，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To close a loop on the firing piece, something I was thinking about while you were talking is there's a lot of layoffs happening right now. When you're letting go of like a thousand people, you can't really be their agent unless you've seen that happen. Do you have any advice for just like there's a large layoff how you could do this?
turns.zh: 最后再谈谈裁员的事。听你讲的时候我在想，现在有很多裁员行动。当你要裁掉上千人时，除非你亲眼目睹过这种情况，否则你很难充当他们的代理人。对于大规模裁员，你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Absolutely you can be their agent, not you personally, but they each have a manager and the manager usually has 12 reports and they're rarely letting go more than 50% at a time. That means six people that they've got to be the agent of maximum. Yes, each manager can be the agent for six people. My companies have done a lot of layoffs and here's why. Back in March of 2020, there was a chance that the world economy was imploding. Now of course, by April and May we realized that wasn't the case, that the tech world kept going, in fact, it was even flourishing.
turns.zh: 当然可以充当他们的代理人，不是你个人，而是他们每人都有一个经理，而经理通常有12个下属，裁员时一次性裁掉的比例很少超过50%。这意味着每个经理最多只能为6个人充当代理人。我的公司也裁过很多人，原因如下。2020年3月，全球经济曾面临崩盘的风险。当然，到4月和5月，我们意识到情况并非如此，科技行业反而还在蓬勃发展。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: But in March of 2020, we didn't know that. And so you needed, if you were being fiscally responsible, you needed to prepare for that eventuality, so you needed pare costs. 80% of costs in any tech company is payroll, is humans. If you're going to pare costs, you actually have to let go of humans. Almost every one of my companies did. Some on the low side of 5%, some on the high side. One company that is a hotel company let go of 40% because it looked like their business was about to get obliterated and the results were crazy. Within 60 days of each layoff, the CEO reported back to me: It's insane. I don't know how this happened, but the company's now operating better. I'm not talking on a relative scale, I'm talking on an absolute scale. We're putting out more features, more code. Our NPS is up, whatever it is, whatever department is performing better. The only answer for it was we've got less people, so this coordination issue is reduced.
turns.zh: 然而，在2020年3月，我们并不知道这些情况。因此，如果你要做到财务上的负责任，就必须为这种可能性做好准备，因此你需要削减成本。在任何科技公司中，80%的成本都是人力成本。如果你要削减成本，就不得不裁减员工。我的大多数公司都这么做了。有些公司裁减了5%左右，有些则高达40%。一家酒店公司裁减了40%员工，因为当时看似他们的业务即将被彻底摧毁，结果却出乎意料。在每次裁员后的60天内，CEO都会向我汇报：太疯狂了。我不知道这是怎么发生的，但公司现在运营得更好了。我不是在说相对的改进，而是绝对的提升。我们推出了更多功能，写出了更多代码。我们的净推荐值（NPS）提升了，无论哪个部门表现得都更出色。唯一的解决之道就是减少人员，这样就能减少协调问题。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Then now in May, June of this year, we had this huge reset of valuations where growth tech stocks dropped by 50 to 90% value and all of a sudden, which we're still in and we don't know how long this can last, it's all based on interest rates so it's likely that growth stocks will be at these valuations until interest rates come back down again, which could be two to three years. These companies now they can go raise money, but it's going to be at a big down round and down rounds are very painful. So now these companies have to make sure that they don't need to raise money in the next three years. They've got to conserve cash once again.
turns.zh: 如今在今年5月和6月，我们经历了估值的大幅调整，成长型科技股的估值暴跌50%至90%，而且这种情况仍在持续，我们不知道会持续多久，这完全取决于利率，因此成长型股票的估值可能会一直维持在当前水平，直到利率再次回升，这可能需要两到三年的时间。这些公司现在可以去融资，但会面临大幅降价，而降价融资对公司来说非常痛苦。因此，这些公司必须确保未来三年内不需要融资，他们必须再次节省现金。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Here we are, we're in the land of layoffs again, but this time it's different. This time these CEOs know that the company actually gets better. And the CEOs that have never done this before, I simply connect them with the CEOs who have done this before and then they get convinced like, oh man, my company will be better. And now this time, people have been even more aggressive. We've had companies that have laid off 50% of the company and the results have been frankly, phenomenal.
turns.zh: 如今我们又回到了裁员的时代，但这次情况不同。这一次，这些CEO知道公司实际上会变得更好。那些从未经历过裁员的CEO，我会把他们和有过裁员经验的CEO联系起来，然后他们就会被说服，哦，天哪，我的公司会变得更好的。而这一次，人们更加激进了。我们有公司裁减了50%的员工，结果坦白说非常惊人。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: But the key to doing it well is there has to be a humane delivery. The biggest marker that I've seen between a botched layoff and a successful layoff is at the moment someone hears that they no longer have a job, did they hear it from their manager in a one-on-one? If that's when they heard it, it'll be okay. But if they heard it in an email, in a group chat, in any kind of thing where they were sitting next to or they're hearing it along with other people, it wasn't personalized, it wasn't one-on-one, that is terrible. That's when people get really angry and that's when they start going on Twitter and going to newspapers and et cetera because it feels dehumanizing. It feels like you didn't give a shit about me. You didn't even have the courtesy to tell me to my face. Of course, there's no way to allow that person to express their emotions because they're in a group. That's the most important thing.
turns.zh: 但做好这件事的关键在于要做到人性化交付。我见过裁员失败和成功的最大区别在于，当有人得知自己失业时，是经理一对一告知的吗？如果是这样，那还好。但如果是通过邮件、群聊，或者在任何他们身边有其他人听到的场合告知的，那就糟糕了。这不是个性化的，不是一对一的，这太可怕了。这会让人们非常生气，他们会上推特、找媒体等等，因为这让人感到不人道。感觉你根本不在乎我。你甚至连当面告诉我都没有。当然，在集体场合你没法让那个人表达自己的情绪。这才是最重要的。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: The second thing is then later, so tactically, this is how it happens. You have an inner circle. I think that inner circle should include all managers in the company and you say, this is how much we need to let go. Here's how much each of you needs to let go. First of all, you don't say to each department head or team leader, manager, tell me who you can let go because they'll all say nobody. You actually have to give them numbers. You have to let this dollar amount go or this many people go, dollar amount is better because if you say people, then they'll just let go of the cheapest people, the most junior, and often the most junior are the ones that are actually doing the most work. You want it to be dollars because that's actually really what you're trying to save. You're trying to save dollars.
turns.zh: 接下来是后续的策略部分。首先，建立一个核心团队。我认为这个核心团队应该包括公司的所有管理层。然后，你要明确告知每个人需要裁减的数量。比如，你不能对每个部门主管或团队领导说："告诉我你能裁掉多少人？"因为他们都会回答"没人"。相反，你需要给出具体的数字——比如需要裁减多少金额，或者裁减多少人。用金额来衡量更合适，因为如果只说裁减人数，团队可能会优先裁掉成本最低、资历最浅的员工，而这些人往往正是真正承担大量工作的人。你需要用具体的金额来衡量，这样才能真正节省开支。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: So, you say you have to save this many dollars, come up with a number, they quickly come back with a number. You don't want to have department heads choose for managers because if you have a team lead and all of a sudden they're told to let go these three people, the team lead will go, that was crazy. Those are my three best people. So you want to let each manager choose and that doesn't need to take long. That could take 48 hours.
turns.zh: 接下来，你设定一个需要节省的金额目标，并给出具体数字。部门主管们很快就会给出他们的裁减方案。但你不想让部门主管替经理做决定——比如，如果一个团队领导突然被告知要裁掉三个人，他可能会抗议："这太疯狂了！那可是我手下最优秀的三个人！"所以你要让每个经理自行选择裁减人选，而这个过程不必耗时太久，比如48小时即可。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Then you move to implementation. At implementation, you spend the morning and have each manager reach out to people and just Slack them say, "Hey, can I talk to you for 15 minutes?" And then they have these meetings back-to-back-to-back or as close as they can and they deliver the news, the difficult conversation that we talked about before. "It's going to be a difficult conversation. I'm letting you go. I imagine this feels crappy or feels like worse than that. This is horrible. If you're willing to share your feelings and I want to be your agent now. I don't have time to do it now, but I'd like to schedule with you another hour tomorrow, the next day whenever, so that we can go and dig in and I can help be your agent."
turns.zh: 实施阶段的工作重点在于：上午让每个经理逐一联系员工，发送Slack消息：“嘿，能占用你15分钟吗？”然后他们会连续召开一系列会议，传递这个令人不快的消息——即艰难的裁员谈话。“这会是一次艰难的对话。我要裁掉你。我知道这感觉很糟糕，甚至更糟。这太不公平了。如果你愿意分享你的感受，我愿意做你的倾诉对象。虽然我现在没时间，但明天或后天我会再安排一小时的沟通时间，让我们深入探讨，帮助你应对。”

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Then, that takes the morning. By the afternoon, you've scheduled an all hands for the stay team. With the stay team, you'd tell them what had just occurred and you answer their questions. The questions are almost always around fear. Like, "Holy shit, is this going to happen to me? Did these people even get feedback that they weren't performing? Does this mean that we're dying as a company and that we're going to implode?" You have to address each one of these questions and hopefully the answer is: no, to the first one, is this going to happen to me? No, this isn't. We cut deep so that we only cut once. The people to your left and right and you, you are the state team. This is the team that we're going to building the company with going forward. It's important to be able to say that. You actually want to cut deep because cutting two times or three times creates PTSD in an organization. It's trauma one, trauma two, trauma three. Now they're like, ah, it's just going to keep happening.
turns.zh: 整个上午都在进行这项工作。下午，你会为留任团队召开全体会议。向留任团队说明刚刚发生的事，并回答他们的疑问。这些疑问几乎都围绕着恐惧心理，比如：“天啊，这会发生在我身上吗？这些人被裁前有得到反馈吗？这是否意味着公司即将倒闭？”你必须逐一解答这些问题，并确保给出令人安心的答案：不，裁员不会波及你。我们一次性裁减到位，让你安心工作。你左右的同事和自己，都是核心团队成员，未来公司将与你们共同成长。这一点至关重要。要强调裁员的决断性，避免反复折腾——一次裁员即可，否则会让组织陷入创伤循环，形成“创伤一”、“创伤二”、“创伤三”的恶性循环，最终员工会认为裁员永无止境。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Then, the third piece is, and this not everybody does, if you don't do this, your company within 60 days will be performing better. If you do this, your company within two weeks will be performing better because people now, the stay team, they feel sadness, they feel anger, they feel fear. Yes, you addressed their questions in the all hands, but not fully because some people didn't even talk in the all hands.
turns.zh: 然后，第三点是——虽然不是每个人都会这么做，但如果你不这么做，你的公司在60天内业绩就会提升。如果你这么做了，你的公司在两周内业绩就会提升，因为现在留任团队的成员，他们感到悲伤、愤怒和恐惧。是的，你在全员大会上回答了他们的问题，但并不充分，因为有些人甚至在会上没有发言。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: So, what you do is with each and every person on the stay team, you have a one-on-one with their manager for one hour and all the manager does is say, "I'd like to know your thoughts and feelings," and the person shares and then all the manager does is make them feel heard. I think what you're telling me is you feel sad because your three buddies are now no longer here and you feel anger because you think this is bullshit and you think why did we hire this many people if we're going to fire them? That was just irresponsible. You feel fear because you're not sure if the company's going to implode or if your job is safe. Is that right? And they're like, "Yes."
turns.zh: 所以，你要做的是与留任团队的每一个人进行一对一的沟通，每次一小时，经理只需说一句：“我想了解你的想法和感受。”然后让对方分享心声，接着经理要确保让对方感受到被倾听。我想你说的是，你感到悲伤，因为你的三个好友现在不在了，感到愤怒，因为你觉得这太不靠谱了，如果要裁员为什么要招这么多人？这太不负责任了。你感到恐惧，因为不确定公司是否会崩盘，或者你的工作是否安全。对吧？他们回答：“是的。”

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: It doesn't take away the emotion entirely, but it knocks it down by a good 25%, which is enough that the person won't do something rash, they won't quit, they won't stop working, they won't say bad shit to other people, and it allows them to accelerates their recovery. Within two weeks, they're now seeing how the company's operating better and morale then comes up and the company's now performing better than it was before. So, three elements.
turns.zh: 这并不能完全消除情绪，但能将其抑制25%，这足以让人们不会做出冲动之举，比如辞职、停止工作、说坏话等，同时也能帮助他们加速恢复。两周后，他们会发现公司运营得更好了，士气也随之提升，业绩比之前更出色了。所以，这就是三个关键点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was thousands of dollars of advice I think, in just five to 10 minutes.
turns.zh: 我认为这价值数千美元的建议，仅需5到10分钟就能提供。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: That's after having probably gone through this with CEOs maybe 40 times and iterating AB testing, and what's the difference, and what works well, and what didn't work well. Yeah, I can't imagine there's somewhat out there who has advised more people through a layoff process, certainly in the tech world, than I have. I'm not saying I'm proud of that, but it just is.
turns.zh: 这是在与CEO们反复探讨这个问题40多次之后，通过AB测试、对比效果、总结经验得出的。是的，我无法想象还有谁比我更频繁地为科技行业的裁员过程提供建议。我不是说我为此感到自豪，但事实就是如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a fun place to be. As you were talking, I was thinking a little bit about Twitter and Elon and the experience that's going through right now. It feels like on the one hand, he's letting go of a lot of people, which matches kind of your advice. On the other hand, not being handled too well. I think it's emails and just a lot of random quick things. What's your perspective on this whole thing?
turns.zh: 这真是个有趣的领域。你说话的时候，我就在想推特和埃隆（Elon），以及他目前正在经历的状况。一方面，他裁掉了很多人，与你的建议不谋而合；另一方面，他处理得不太好。比如发邮件和很多随意的快速通知。你对这整件事有什么看法？

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: I haven't been following it directly, so I don't know how he's implementing the layoffs or how much he's doing. Frankly, just haven't been following it at all. But here's the sad reality, even if it's handled incredibly poorly, the company ends up performing better. It just takes a little longer for people to recover, for the stay team to recover emotionally. But the worst case scenario, it's handled terribly, within two months, the company will be performing better.
turns.zh: 我没有直接关注，所以不知道他如何实施裁员或裁员规模有多大。坦白说，我根本没有关注。但悲哀的现实是，即使处理得极其糟糕，公司最终也会表现得更好。只是人们需要更长时间来恢复，留任团队需要更长时间在情感上恢复。但最坏的情况是，处理得极其糟糕，两个月内公司也会表现得更好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fascinating. That's actually a good segue to this last topic I wanted to touch on, which something that I think you have a lot of thoughts on is building new products within a larger company and innovating inside of a larger kind of scaled company, and especially the challenges around that. What are your thoughts on just how to do this well, how to innovate within a larger company?
turns.zh: 太有意思了。这正好引出我接下来想谈的最后一个话题。我认为你对在大公司内开发新产品和进行创新，特别是其中的挑战，应该有很多自己的见解。那么，如何才能做好这件事，在大公司内部实现创新呢？

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: I can tell you the short version, but I'll tell you the long version. The long version is that this was a real problem for everyone I was coaching and I didn't know the answer. But it was obvious that YC startups were crushing and just iterating so much faster. And then I had the thought, well, why not just create your own YC startup and have it crush you but you own it? It, of course, has to really look like a YC startup. It has to have a founder mentality person as the head of the team, someone who's willing to just break glass and just won't stop until they run through the brick wall. It's actually pretty easy to find founder mentality folks. You just literally go to the YC alumni list and the ones whose startups failed, perfect, they're available and they are founder types and now they want to join a company that's actually succeeding because they realize how hard it is to create something on their own, but they still have the mentality.
turns.zh: 我可以简单说一下，但更详细的解释如下。这对所有我指导过的创业者来说都是个现实难题，我当时也找不到答案。但很明显，YC孵化的初创公司在创新方面表现出色，而且迭代速度极快。于是我突然想到，何不创建自己的YC初创公司，让它来挑战现有业务，同时又由你自己掌控？当然，这家公司必须真正具备YC初创公司的特质。团队负责人必须具备创业者思维，愿意突破常规，永不止步地攻克难关。这样的创业者并不难找——直接从YC校友名单中寻找那些创业失败的人即可。他们既有创业精神，又渴望加入成功的公司，因为他们深知独自创业的艰难，但仍保持着创业者的思维模式。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Then you want to keep the team really small because then they can, again, there's no buy-in required, like everyone's on the same page with the same information. We started testing that and it worked, and then I thought, well wait a second. The reason that a big company has a hard time innovating, it's because once a product is scaled, it's now got millions of users. So you have two things that you need to make sure stay true every day: the site is up and running and there's no security breach. Every time you add code, you've got to test it thoroughly to make sure it doesn't take down either one of those. The review process is insane.
turns.zh: 接下来要保持团队规模极小，这样每个人都能共享同样的信息，无需协调。我们的尝试证明了这一点确实有效。但随后我又意识到，大公司创新困难的根本原因在于，一旦产品规模化后，就会有数百万用户。于是你必须每天确保两件事：网站正常运行且不存在安全漏洞。每次添加代码时，都必须进行全面测试，确保不会影响这两项核心功能。这样的审核流程简直令人抓狂。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: So now you're innovating, you're writing prototype code on new features. You can't get it approved it takes so long. That's what you're trying to decouple and you're trying to create an entity that isn't touching the core code, but you also don't want to have to go through the approval process of the product team or the head of product. That takes way too long, as well. That's why it has to be a small team that reports to outside of EPD. It can't report to the head of engineering, head of product, head of design, it can't. It's got to go outside, usually directly to the CEO. That's the only other place to report that's outside.
turns.zh: 当你正在创新、编写新功能的原型代码时，却要花很长时间才能获得批准。这正是你试图分离的部分——你需要创建一个不触及核心代码的实体，同时又无需经过产品团队或产品负责人的审批流程。这也太耗时了。因此，这个团队必须小型化，并直接向CEO汇报，而不是工程、产品或设计负责人。这是唯一可以汇报的非内部部门。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Then I had this idea, well wait a second, there's also a brand question and so why don't you create an entirely new name for this product that isn't the core, the base business? Why don't you actually just create its own C corp? Why don't you make it so clear that this is its own entity? So I wrote this whole thing up and created its own C corp. I shared this with a few people and one CEO said to me, "Matt, this sounds radical and sounds like it could work, but is anyone actually doing this?" I thought to myself, oh shit, no, nobody's actually doing this. Nobody that I know has created new C Corps for the entities, the new products they're developing.
turns.zh: 然后我又想到，既然如此，品牌定位也是个问题。为何不为这个非核心产品创建一个全新的名称？为何不直接成立一家独立的C corp公司？为何不明确标示这是独立实体？于是我详细规划了整个方案，创建了独立的C corp公司。把方案分享给几位CEO后，其中一位问我：“马特，这听起来很激进，也许可行，但真的有人这么做吗？”我心想，天哪，没有人这么做。至少我认识的没有人为新开发的产品创建独立的C corp公司。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Then 30 days later, I got in a call with Wei Deng. I told you before, I'm a huge fan, and we talked about product and I shared with her this write up. She's like, "Oh yeah, that's what I do." She said, "I created five C Corps in the last two months." I was like, "What? Someone's actually doing it." I was like, "Well, what are the results?" She's like, "They're fantastic." She goes, "The team doesn't worry about trying shit because they know that it doesn't hurt our core brand, and so they're iterating fast." And she said, "Not only do I do that, I actually have two teams, independent, working on each new product. One I have is more engineering focused, they build custom code. The other is more sort of customer relationship-focused and maybe they don't even have engineers and they build a manual solution or they use off the shelf products to build a solution, and just see which one makes more progress faster." Wow, insane. That's why, again, I have so much respect for Wei.
turns.zh: 30天后，我和魏登通了电话。我之前跟你说过，我是她的超级粉丝。我们聊了产品方面的事情，我把那份写作分享给她。她说：“哦，对啊，这就是我的工作。”她说：“过去两个月我创建了五家C类公司。”我说：“什么？真有人这么做啊。”我问：“那结果如何？”她回答：“效果棒极了。” 她接着说：“团队不担心尝试新东西，因为他们知道这不会损害我们的核心品牌，所以能快速迭代。” 她还说：“我不仅这么做，我还有两个独立团队在开发新产品。一个团队更侧重工程，负责定制代码开发；另一个团队更专注客户关系，可能没有工程师，他们会用手动解决方案或现成产品搭建方案，然后看看哪个进展更快。” 哇，太不可思议了。这就是为什么我对魏登如此敬佩。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When I think about these ideas, I think of the NPE team at Facebook and I think it's called Area 21 at Google, which works on new ideas and I don't know if anything amazing has come out of those groups maybe, I don't know. But it feels like the missing piece, and you didn't mention this piece, is feeling like there's a huge upside if you get something. Like founders having equity of their company feels like such a motivator. I could become a billionaire if this works out, versus I'm helping my startup in some small incremental way. Is that an important piece or do you think it's not critical?
turns.zh: 当我思考这些理念时，会想到Facebook的NPE团队和谷歌的Area 21，后者专注于新创意项目。我不知道这些团队是否产出过惊艳成果，但感觉缺失的关键环节在于，当成功时能获得巨大回报。比如创始人持有公司股权，这对激励作用巨大。如果项目成功，我就能成为亿万富翁；而如果只是以微小增量方式助力初创公司，激励效果就大打折扣。这是关键因素吗？还是说不重要？

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: I'm going to be radical here. I don't think it matters at all. I think that what really motivates people is building shit that gets used in the world. I think people will say, and they'll fight for equity and money, but in the end, that's not what actually motivates them. Because I've seen this work in companies where they don't have big equity, but they have autonomy, they have ownership, not equity ownership, ownership over decision making, ownership over creation. That's what I think people want. Amazon does this. They're not giving their people... Amazon's famous for being cheap bastards, but someone has a great idea, okay, here's 5 million bucks, go do. Amazon is definitely innovating successfully.
turns.zh: 我要大胆说一句，我认为这根本无关紧要。我认为真正激励人们的是创造出能被世界使用的产品。人们会争取股权和金钱，但归根结底，这些并非核心动力。因为我见过有些公司没有高额股权，但赋予员工自主权和决策权——这才是人们真正想要的。亚马逊就是如此。他们不以慷慨闻名，但如果有人有好点子，他们会说：“给你500万美元，去做吧。” 亚马逊无疑在创新方面很成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What about the flip side of that of not necessarily the huge upside, but the I'm staking everything on this startup, I need this to work, this is my thing, my name's on the line. I feel like that's a big motivator also for founders, like I'm not going to give up this feeling of grit. Is that important?
turns.zh: 那反面的情况呢？不一定是巨大回报，但可能是孤注一掷：我把一切都押在这家初创公司上，必须成功，这关乎我的名声。我觉得这对创始人也是巨大的动力，比如我不会放弃这种拼劲。这种拼劲很重要吗？

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Yeah, it's also fear. It's fear, which is like if this doesn't work, I'm screwed. Fear, frankly, is an excellent motivator. It gets people to move fast and move hard. The only problem with fear is it's also corrosive, so it eats out my insides as I go along. It makes it that I don't enjoy life, but it's highly motivated. Now, I think joy is actually even more motivating or they say it's as motivating, but it's noncorrosive, so I can last much longer if I'm doing something for joy. Fear is short term, extreme motivation. It's adrenaline. Joy is long term, consistent motivation that also allows me to look back on my life and go, wow, that was a great life. So yes, that is effective motivation, but I don't recommend putting oneself in that position to get motivated.
turns.zh:
是啊，这也是恐惧。恐惧就像是，如果这件事不成功，我就完蛋了。说实话，恐惧是一种极好的动力。它能让人行动迅速、全力以赴。但问题是，恐惧也是具腐蚀性的，它会慢慢侵蚀我的内心，让我无法享受生活。不过它确实能带来强大的动力。

而我认为快乐实际上更能激发动力，或者说同样能激发动力，但它没有腐蚀性。所以只要是为了快乐去做事，我就能坚持得更久。恐惧是短期的、极端的动力，比如肾上腺素激增。而快乐是长期的、持续的动力，甚至能让我回首人生时感叹：哇，这真是精彩的一生。所以没错，恐惧确实是有效的动力，但我不建议用这种方式来激励自己。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For companies that want to try this method that you're describing, is there a curriculum document for this approach out there?
turns.zh: 对于想尝试你所描述的这种方法的公司来说，是否有相关的课程文件可以参考？

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: There is.
turns.zh: 有的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, we'll link to that. Are there any other companies that are doing this well that come to mind? You mentioned Amazon, Clipboard Health.
turns.zh: 好的，我们会提供链接。你能否列举一些在这方面做得很好的公司？你提到了亚马逊和Clipboard Health。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: In my portfolio, I know Scale and Attentive Mobile are both doing this well. More and more companies that I coach are starting to do this because I have more and more examples of it working well, so more and more companies are then copying. I don't have other names offhand that I can share though.
turns.zh: 在我的投资组合中，Scale和Attentive Mobile在这方面都做得很好。越来越多的我指导的公司也开始采用这种方法，因为我有越来越多的成功案例，所以越来越多的公司开始效仿。不过我现在没法随口列出其他公司的名字。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What was that first company? Scale?
turns.zh: 第一个公司是什么？Scale？

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Scale.
turns.zh: Scale。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. Is that Scale AI?
turns.zh: 不错。是Scale AI吗？

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. I love that. Love that founder. Maybe a last question, something that I noted just in case we had a little more time is around energy audit. This is something that you advise folks to understand what gives them energy, what zaps their energy, can you talk a bit about that?
turns.zh: 好的，不错。我很欣赏那个创始人。最后一个问题，我记下来的以防时间不够用，是关于能量审计的。你建议人们了解什么能给他们带来能量，什么会消耗他们的能量，能否谈谈这个话题？

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Sure. It turns out that what we're really good at is what we love and what we love is often space and time disappear when we do it. Therefore, we actually probably don't even value it because it comes so easily to us that we don't ascribe value. Whereas things that we don't love but we're good at, we often ascribe value there and other people want us to do those things because they're often creating value for the whole team or the family or the group.
turns.zh: 当然。事实证明，我们真正擅长的事情往往是我们热爱的，而当我们热爱某件事时，时间和精力就会消失。因此，我们可能甚至不重视它，因为它对我们来说太容易了，以至于我们不赋予它价值。而那些我们不热爱但擅长的事情，我们往往会赋予它价值，其他人也希望我们去做这些事情，因为这些事情往往为整个团队、家庭或群体创造价值。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: There are four zones I posit and I learned this from Diana Chapman at Conscious Leadership Group. I don't know where she learned it from, but almost everything that I have, I poached from somebody, but at least I tell you where I poached it from. The concept is you have four zones.
turns.zh: 我提出了四个区域，这个概念来自于Conscious Leadership Group的Diana Chapman。我不知道她从哪里学到的，但我所拥有的大多数东西都是从别人那里借鉴来的，但至少我会告诉你我从哪里借鉴的。这个概念是，你有四个区域。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Zone one is your incompetence, you're not good at it, someone's better at it than you. That's like fixing a car. You should let someone else do that.
turns.zh: 第一个区域是你的无能区，你不擅长它，有人比你更擅长它。比如修车。你应该让别人来做。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Second is your zone of competence, you're fine, you can do it fine. But so can somebody else do it fine. Like cleaning your house. Yes, you could do it, but it would take a lot of time and you're not creating that much value. You should let someone else do that.
turns.zh: 第二个区域是你的胜任区，你做得还可以，但其他人也能做得很好。比如打扫你的房子。是的，你可以做，但会花很多时间，而且你创造不了那么多价值。你应该让别人来做。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Third zone, your zone of excellence. This is something that you're uniquely good at, but you don't love it. This is the danger zone. This is likely what you're getting paid for and you're likely to getting paid a lot of money for it. Other people want you to do it. You are creating value, but it's also sucking the life force out of you and it doesn't allow you to become amazing and create massive value.
turns.zh: 第三个区域——你的卓越区。这是你独具专长的领域，但你却并不热爱它。这是一个危险区。很可能这正是你领取高薪的所在，也是他人期望你去做的工作。你创造了价值，但同时也在耗尽自身精力，无法实现自我超越与价值最大化。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Then there's your zone of genius. This is the thing you do that's uniquely good in the world and you don't even notice that you're doing it because you love it so much. The key is to go and look at your day. How do you move into the zone of genius? It's not that you figure out what it is and do more of that, it's that you figure out what it isn't and eliminate that and then naturally, you'll be drawn toward what it is that you love.
turns.zh: 接下来是你的天赋区。这是你独一无二擅长之事，而你甚至未曾意识到自己在做这件事，因为你深深热爱它。关键在于审视你的日常生活。如何进入天赋区？并非去发掘你擅长之事并加大投入，而是识别并消除不擅长之处，随后你自然会被吸引至真正热爱之事。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: What I do with the energy audit is you go through a calendar, two weeks of a calendar, a representative two weeks and you first look at all the meetings you have, but then you fill in there's time in between meetings. What were you actually doing? Take your best guess, write it in and then hour by hour, take a green marker and a red marker and each hour from Monday, 8:00 AM to 6:00 PM and the same thing each day for two weeks, each hour ask yourself at the end of that hour, did I have more energy or less energy?
turns.zh: 我在能量审计中会这样操作：通览两周日程表，选择具有代表性的两周。首先审视所有会议安排，但要填补会议间隙的时间空白。你实际在做什么？尽可能猜测并记录下来，然后逐小时追踪，从周一上午8点到下午6点，连续两周每小时提问：我此时精力充沛还是疲惫？

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: If it's more energy, you mark it green. If it's neutral or negative, you mark it red. Then, once you've done that for two weeks, you look at all the reds and say what's with the themes here? Oh, one on ones with people who are no longer by direct reports, team meetings where nothing was prepared in advance and everything was verbal. Recruiting meetings, interviews with people that we didn't end up hiring. Informational interviews from people that wanted to meet me and just know me but provide no value to me. These are all things that are energy draining.
turns.zh: 若精力充沛，标记绿色；若中性或消极，标记红色。完成两周审计后，分析所有红色标记，归纳出共同主题。例如：与已不再直属的下属开会、毫无准备的团队会议、未录用人员的招聘面谈、仅想了解我却毫无价值的信息性访谈等。这些都是精力消耗源。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Great. Now what you do is you go through each one of them and say, one, do I need to do this at all? Does it need to be done? If the answer is no, just cancel it. Two, it needs to be done, but someone else can do it. Great, delegate it to them. Three, and this is the most common, it needs to be done and only I can do it. Great, then the question is, what would make it exquisite? Well, it's the exec team meeting. I'm the CEO, I have to be in it. Well, what would make it exquisite?
turns.zh: 接下来要逐一分析：一、是否有必要参与？若否，直接取消。二、必须参与，但他人可代劳？委派给他人。三、最常见情况：必须亲自参与。那么如何提升质量？以高管会议为例，我作为CEO必须出席。如何让它卓越起来？

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: You know what would be exquisite? It would be exquisite if everyone pre-prepared their update, which said how they're doing against their priorities, regular green, what they did last week, what they're going to do this week, and then they pre-route any problems they saw in the company and any proposed solution they had for those problems. If everyone did that, then we could spend the first 15 minutes of the meeting just reading, processing the decisions and we could take a three hour meeting down to a 45 minute meeting. Great, go write that up, share it with a group and say, hey gang, this is what would make this meaning exquisite for me. What do you guys think?
turns.zh: 你会发现：若所有人提前准备更新报告，清晰展示对优先事项的达成进度、上周工作回顾、本周计划，并提前预判公司问题并提出解决方案——所有人都能做到这些——那么我们就能将三小时会议缩短至45分钟。整理这些建议，与团队分享并征求意见：这将让会议对我而言变得卓越，你们怎么看？

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Nine out of 10 times people look at it and go, yeah, that would be amazing because they're feeling the same way. Then you go with a new methodology and it turns out to be great. That's how you take what you do each day from a lot of energy draining things into open space or energy raising things which will then allow you to start doing more and more of the things that you love. You keep doing this energy audit repeatedly, 1, 2, 3 times until your calendar is 80% green. Once that happens, magic will occur. All of a sudden, your life will become phenomenal and you will start to create massive value. I did it. That's what happened to me.
turns.zh: 十有八九，人们看完后会想：“嗯，这确实很棒，因为他们也有同样的感受。”然后你尝试一种新方法，结果效果出奇地好。正是这样，你能把日常工作从耗费精力的任务转变为激发能量的活动，从而能投入更多时间做自己热爱的事。反复进行能量审计，1、2、3次直到日程表里80%都是绿色任务。这样一来，奇迹就会发生。突然间，你的生活会变得无比美好，开始创造巨大价值。我就这么做过，这就是我的经历。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I did that too actually, a simpler version where I just paid attention to what gave me energy and what didn't give me energy when I was on this journey post Airbnb and I thought I was wanted to start a company, I thought I wanted to do some advising and consulting and I realized none of that gives me energy, but writing interesting things that people like, that was fun. So I just kind of doubled down on that path and had no idea was going to make any money and it ended up making money and that's what I do now. So yeah, two thumbs up for this method and it's a more sophisticated version, which I like.
turns.zh: 其实我也这么做过，不过更简单些。离开Airbnb后，我关注什么能给我能量，什么不能。当初我想创办公司、做顾问咨询，结果发现这些都无法激发我的能量。倒是写人们喜欢读的有趣内容挺有意思的。于是我专注于这条路，不在乎能否赚钱，结果钱反倒赚到了，这就是我现在的生活。所以我要为这种方法点赞，它更高级，我很喜欢。

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: Right on. That's also trusting that there will be, if you need to monetize, eventually you will be able to monetize, but you got to start with doing the thing you love first.
turns.zh: 太对了。这也需要相信，如果需要变现，总会有办法的。但首先得专注于自己热爱的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. Yeah, I feel like there's a lot of people on Twitter and newsletters that are just doing it because they think this is something they will enjoy and other people are doing it. But I find that with this content life, you get on this treadmill where you have to continue producing things and if you don't actually enjoy it and it's not interesting to you, you end up just building this job for yourself that is no fun at all. Extra important if you're kind of going down this path.
turns.zh: 对啊。我发现推特和新闻简报里很多人做事只是因为觉得别人在做，自己也该试试。但我发现这种内容创作就像跑步机模式，必须持续产出。如果不享受这个过程，毫无乐趣可言。尤其是当你正走这条路时，更要注意这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One quick question I had along these lines is you're talking about how you focus on yourself and your energy and what works for you or not. And I was like, do these collide with other people on your team because they maybe get energy from something you don't? But your point is that oftentimes, everyone's like, "Yes, this is good for me too. We should do this because it's going to help everybody feel better."
turns.zh: 我有个相关问题：你提到专注自我、能量匹配、什么对你有效。但这会和团队其他人产生冲突吗？毕竟他们可能从你不喜欢的方面获取能量？但你的观点是，通常大家都会说：“对，我也喜欢这样。我们应该这么做，因为能让大家感觉更好。”

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: That's exactly right. I remember one time we did this energy audit process, I did it with Henrique and Pedro from Brex and it was revolutionary for them. It caused them to change how the two of them operated together. They realized one really enjoyed the internal meetings and the other really enjoyed the external meetings, so well great, let's just do that. It changed the trajectory of the company so much so that they said, "Matt, would you please come in and do this energy audit with all of our managers?" And we did. We did a big group thing and what they found was that process also changes the trajectory of the company because for everything that you don't enjoy but needs to get done, there's someone out there that loves to do it. You just got to find out who it is, and that's what happened.
turns.zh: 完全正确。我记得有次和Brex的Henrique、Pedro做能量审计，对他们来说是革命性的。它改变了他们的合作模式。他们发现一个喜欢内部会议，另一个喜欢外部会议，于是决定专注各自擅长的。这彻底改变了公司发展轨迹，以至于他们邀请我给所有经理做审计。我们成功了。结果发现这个过程同样能改变公司命运，因为对于你不喜欢但必须做的事，总有热爱它的人存在。你只需找到他们，这就是故事的结局。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was just talking to my mom who's a CPA and I'm like, "Do you even enjoy this job you're doing?" She's like, "I love it. I love doing taxes. It's so interesting." I'm like, I'm so happy somebody out there enjoys this. I would pay anything for someone to take this off my plate. You can charge me. Because my mom does my taxes.
turns.zh: 我刚和身为注册会计师的妈妈聊天，问她：“你真的喜欢现在这份工作吗？”她回答：“我超爱这份工作的。我喜欢做税务规划，这太有趣了。” 我说：“真高兴还有人喜欢这份工作。我愿意花大价钱找人替我处理这些事。你尽管收费吧，反正我妈帮我做税务呢。”

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: That's exactly right.
turns.zh: 说得太对了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Matt, any final thoughts you want to share before we wrap up?
turns.zh: 马特，在结束前你还有什么想分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Matt Mochary
turns.en: This was fun. Thanks, Lenny. I appreciate this.
turns.zh: 这次聊天很愉快。谢谢你，莱尼。我很感激。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Super fun. I feel like a sign of a great conversation is it feels like we've been talking for maybe five minutes, but also a lifetime. Maybe we'll do this again. There's like a million other questions I'd love to get into, but until then, where can folks find you online if they want to reach out and learn more and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 超级有趣。我觉得一次好的对谈，应该让人感觉聊了五分钟，却又像过了整个人生。说不定我们还能再聊一次。还有无数其他问题我想深入探讨，但现在，如果听众想了解更多信息，可以在哪里找到你？

turns.en: Where can people find me? I don't know. Don't find me. I won't be able to respond. I get too many inbounds and I can't respond to them. In terms of people helpful to me, just read the content and use it and don't pay me to coach you. Just do it on your own because you don't need to pay me to coach you.
turns.zh: 哪里能找到我？我不知道。别找我。我回复不过来了。收到的私信太多了，实在没法一一回复。至于如何能帮到你，就多看看我的内容，运用起来吧，不用花钱请我指导你自己就能做到。

turns.en: I love that. It's the first time someone's like, "Do not reach out. I got it all for you online." We'll link to the show notes of the doc and everything. Matt, thank you. This was incredible.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这样。这还是第一次有人说：“别找我，我已经把所有资源都放在网上了。” 我们会附上节目笔记和相关文档的链接。马特，谢谢你。这次聊天太棒了。

turns.en: Thank you, Lenny. This was great. Take care.
